topics: 👑 The Ḥasid and the Officer — an a fortiori from a mortal king to the King of kings
🐍 Snake vs. Scorpion — Rav Sheshet limits the mishna; oxen, and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's arvad
🌧️ Where the Additions Go — rain in 'revival of the dead', the request in 'the years', havdala in 'grants knowledge'
🧠 Great Is Knowledge — placed between two Names of God, like the Temple; Rav Aḥa's objection from vengeance
🍷 Havdala Twice — the enactment's history and Rava's ruling that it goes in the Amida and over the cup, like kiddush
🐦 'Your Mercy Reaches the Bird's Nest' — three phrases that get a prayer leader silenced, and the limits of praise

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Danger, Additions, and Heresy in Prayer
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 33a–33b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין עַרְוָד מֵמִית, אֶלָּא הַחֵטְא מֵמִית
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with the ḥasid's answer to the officer whose greeting he ignored: if you would not turn from a mortal king, how could I turn from the King of kings? The Gemara then limits the mishna's 'snake wrapped around his heel' — a scorpion or a charging ox does interrupt prayer — and tells how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa killed a deadly arvad with his heel. A new mishna places the seasonal additions in the Amida: rain, the request for rain, and havdala. That last one launches a long discussion — the history of havdala moving between the Amida and the cup of wine, and what to do when a festival falls right after Shabbat. The final mishna lists the prayer leader who says 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest', 'Your name be mentioned with the good', or 'modim, modim' — and is silenced.

slides.title: 🐍 Which Dangers Interrupt the Amida?
slides.subtitle: The mishna says a snake on the heel does not; the amoraim draw the line

boxes.title: Do not interrupt
items: A snake wrapped around the heel — if you do not provoke it, it will not bite
Objection: one who fell into a pit of snakes is presumed dead! Answer: there the pressure of his fall makes them bite
A ḥasid ignored a Roman officer's greeting and was threatened with death

boxes.title: Interrupt
items: Rav Sheshet: a scorpion — it stings even when undisturbed
Rabbi Yitzḥak: one who sees oxen coming stops; Rav Hoshaya: keep fifty cubits from an innocuous ox, and out of sight of a forewarned one
Rabbi Meir: while the ox's head is in the feed basket, climb to the roof and kick the ladder away. Shmuel: this is for a black ox in Nisan, when Satan dances between its horns

boxes.title: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
items: An arvad was harming people; he asked to see its hole and set his heel over it
It came out, bit him — and died
He carried it to the study hall: 'It is not the arvad that kills, but sin that kills'
'Woe to the man who meets an arvad, and woe to the arvad that meets Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa'

callout.label: The ḥasid's a fortiori:
callout.text: 'Had you been standing before a flesh-and-blood king and a friend greeted you, would you answer?' 'No — they would cut off my head.' 'You feared a king who is here today and in the grave tomorrow; I stood before the King of kings, who lives forever — all the more so!' The officer was appeased and the ḥasid went home in peace.

slides.title: 🌧️ Where Do the Seasonal Additions Belong?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yosef explains the mishna's placements, and the Tosefta tells us what happens when they are forgotten
rows: Might of the rains — 'He makes the wind blow and the rain fall'
Rain is sustenance, so it goes in the blessing of sustenance
Distinguishing requires wisdom; the Rabbis: it is the first weekday blessing
He does not return, because he says it over the cup

callout.label: Great is knowledge:
callout.text: Rav Ami: it heads the weekday blessings and sits between two Names — 'God of knowledge is the Lord' (I Samuel 2:3); one lacking knowledge may not be pitied (Isaiah 27:11). Rabbi Elazar: so does the Temple (Exodus 15:17), hence one with knowledge is as if the Temple were built in his days. Rav Aḥa Karḥina'a objected: then vengeance is great too — 'God of vengeance, Lord' (Psalms 94:1)! Answer: yes, in its place it is great; Ulla: one vengeance for good (Deut. 33:2), one for evil.

slides.title: 🍷 Havdala in the Amida, Over the Cup — or Both?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's history of the enactment and the rulings that follow from it

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Shemen bar Abba to Rabbi Yoḥanan: the Great Assembly instituted blessings, prayers, kiddushim and havdalot — where did they put havdala?

2️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan: at first in the Amida; when the people grew wealthy, over the cup; when they became poor again, back in the Amida — and they said: one who says it in the Amida must also say it over the cup
3️⃣ Rava objects from the Tosefta: omitting havdala does not require repeating the Amida 'because he can say it over the cup' — sounds optional! Answer: read 'because he says it over the cup'

4️⃣ The reverse case: said it over the cup — must he say it in the Amida? Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: a fortiori — if the Amida, the principal enactment, does not exempt the cup, the cup surely does not exempt the Amida

5️⃣ Rav Aḥa Arikha's baraita: 'in this and that — blessings on his head' would be an unnecessary blessing, a violation of 'do not take the Name in vain' (Rav / Reish Lakish / Rabbi Yoḥanan). Emend: 'in this and not in that'
6️⃣ Rav Ḥisda asked Rav Sheshet: erred in both? He returns to the beginning of both. Ravina asked Rava: the halakha? Like kiddush — said in the Amida, it is still said over the cup; so too havdala

callout.label: Kiddush as the model:
callout.text: מָה קִידּוּשׁ אַף עַל גַּב דִּמְקַדֵּשׁ בִּצְלוֹתָא מְקַדֵּשׁ אַכָּסָא, אַף הַבְדָּלָה נָמֵי — the double recitation is the norm, not a redundancy.

slides.title: 🎉 A Festival Right After Shabbat — Whose Havdala?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Zeira on his donkey, Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Avin walking behind, and the precise wording of a tradition

lines.speaker: R' Ḥiyya b. Avin
lines.text: Do you really say in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer — havdala in Thanksgiving — when a festival falls after Shabbat? (There is no 'grants knowledge' in the festival Amida.)

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: 'Halakha' implies a dispute — who disputes? The Rabbis? They argue only the rest of the year. Rabbi Akiva's separate blessing? We never follow him: the Sages instituted eighteen, not nineteen — and here seven, not eight.

lines.speaker: R' Zeira
lines.text: It was not 'halakha' that was said, but 'one is inclined' (מַטִּין).

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Indeed the versions vary: Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi citing Rav — halakha, or some say inclined; Rabbi Yoḥanan — the Rabbis agree; Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba — his view appears correct.

lines.speaker: R' Zeira
lines.text: Hold on to Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba's version — he learns a tradition precisely from his master's mouth, like Raḥava of Pumbedita, who kept Rabbi Yehuda's very word stav for the Temple Mount's double colonnade.

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef
lines.text: I know neither this nor that — but I know that Rav and Shmuel fixed a pearl for us in Babylonia: 'Vatodi'einu'.

callout.label: The pearl:
callout.text: וַתּוֹדִיעֵנוּ ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ אֶת מִשְׁפְּטֵי צִדְקֶךָ… בֵּין קְדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת לִקְדוּשַּׁת יוֹם טוֹב הִבְדַּלְתָּ — 'You have made known to us Your righteous laws… You have distinguished between the holiness of Shabbat and the holiness of the festival' — a havdala woven into the festival's own blessing.

slides.title: 🐦 'Your Mercy Reaches the Bird's Nest' — Why Silence Him?
slides.subtitle: The final mishna of the chapter and Rabbi Ḥanina's warning against piling up praise

nodes.content: 📜 Mishna: one who says 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest', 'Your name be mentioned with the good', or 'modim, modim' — they silence him
✅ 'Modim, modim' looks like two authorities. 'With the good' thanks only for good — but one must bless for the bad as for the good
❓ But the bird's nest — God's mercy on the mother bird (Deut. 22:6–7) — what is wrong with invoking it?

columns.label: One amora
columns.content: It casts jealousy among the works of Creation — as if God favors one creature

columns.label: The other
columns.content: It makes God's attributes into mercy, when they are only decrees

nodes.content: 🧪 A leader before Rabba said 'You pitied the bird's nest, pity us.' Rabba: how well he knows to appease his Master! Abaye: but the mishna silences him! — Rabba only wanted to sharpen Abaye

👑 A leader before Rabbi Ḥanina said 'the great, mighty, awesome, powerful, strong, fearless…' — 'Have you finished all your Master's praises? Even the three we say we could not, had Moses not said them and the Great Assembly not fixed them. A king with a million gold dinars praised for silver — is that not an insult?'

callout.label: Also on the daf:
callout.text: Rabbi Ḥanina: everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven (Deut. 10:12) — a small thing only for Moses, like a man asked for a large vessel he already owns. Rabbi Zeira: saying 'Shema, Shema' is like 'modim, modim'; repeating word by word is merely reprehensible, repeating a whole verse gets him silenced. Rav Pappa asked Abaye: perhaps he lacked focus the first time?

summary.principle: Prayer stands before the King of kings — so it yields only to real danger, holds its enactments precisely, and refuses both heretical hints and inflated praise.

flowSteps.content: 👑 The ḥasid to the officer: you would not turn from a mortal king; I stood before the King of kings
🐍 Snake on the heel — do not stop; scorpion or charging ox — stop. 'Not the arvad but sin kills'
🌧️ Rain in 'revival of the dead', request in 'the years', havdala in 'grants knowledge' (R' Akiva: own blessing; R' Eliezer: Thanksgiving)

columns.content: 🍷 Havdala both in the Amida and over the cup — like kiddush (Rava)
🎉 Festival after Shabbat: inclined to R' Eliezer; Rav and Shmuel's 'Vatodi'einu'

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Silence 'modim modim', 'with the good', and 'bird's nest' — and do not heap praises beyond 'great, mighty, awesome'

quiz.q: Why does Rav Sheshet say one interrupts prayer for a scorpion but not for a snake?
o: A scorpion's sting is always fatal while a snake's is not
A snake will not bite unless it is attacked, but a scorpion stings even when undisturbed
Scorpions are more common in Babylonia than snakes
The mishna explicitly mentions scorpions
quiz.e: The mishna's 'snake wrapped around his heel' is limited to a snake, which does not bite if left alone; a scorpion is liable to sting regardless, so it is a real danger and one stops.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, why was havdala at one point moved from the Amida to the cup of wine?
o: Because the Amida was too long
Because the people became wealthy and could afford wine
Because Rabbi Akiva ruled it must be a separate blessing
Because kiddush was moved at the same time
quiz.e: Initially havdala was fixed in the Amida; when the people became wealthy it was fixed over the cup; when they became poor again it returned to the Amida — and they ruled that one who says it in the Amida must also say it over the cup.

quiz.q: Why is Rabbi Akiva's independent havdala blessing not adopted even on a festival that follows Shabbat?
o: Because Rabbi Akiva later retracted
Because the festival Amida has no blessing of knowledge
Because the Sages instituted seven festival blessings, not eight, just as they instituted eighteen weekday blessings, not nineteen
Because havdala over the cup replaces it
quiz.e: Just as throughout the year we do not follow Rabbi Akiva since the Sages fixed eighteen blessings and not nineteen, on a festival they fixed seven and not eight, so his view is set aside.

quiz.q: What are the two reasons given for silencing one who says 'Your mercy reaches the bird's nest'?
o: It mentions a Torah law in prayer, and it addresses God in the second person
It casts jealousy among the works of Creation, and it presents God's attributes as mercy rather than decrees
It is too long, and it is not in Hebrew
It resembles a Christian prayer, and it repeats a word twice
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin and Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida disagree: one says it engenders jealousy among God's creatures, as if He favors one over another; the other says it turns God's decrees into expressions of mercy.

quiz.q: What was Rabbi Ḥanina's point in comparing God to a king with many thousands of gold dinars who is praised for silver ones?
o: That praise of God should be recited only in the Temple
That heaping up adjectives belittles God, since even 'great, mighty, awesome' are permitted only because Moses said them and the Great Assembly fixed them
That one should praise God with wealth rather than words
That silver blessings are preferable to golden ones
quiz.e: After a leader added 'powerful, strong, fearless, steadfast, honored', Rabbi Ḥanina objected that any list of praises falls infinitely short, like praising a fabulously rich king for his silver; we say only the three Moses said and the Great Assembly instituted.
